generatedProse.concept-context: In psychology, evaluation is where you weigh one explanation against another. A single study rarely settles a question: rival interpretations compete to account for the same evidence. To evaluate is to ask which fits the data better, and why, how large and representative the sample was, whether the effect has replicated, whether a simpler explanation would do. The verdict comes with reasons drawn from the evidence, not from preference.
generatedProse.worked-example:
Two psychology students write about the same interpretation of a well-known finding.

Tom takes the interpretation apart neatly: here is the claim, here is the study offered for it, here is the reasoning. The account is accurate, and it stops there. Tom has analysed the interpretation but not weighed it: there is no sense of how strong it is, or how it stands against any other reading of the same data. This is analysis without evaluation.

Amara goes further. Having seen the parts, she sets this interpretation against a rival one and asks which better accounts for the evidence. The first explains more of the data but rests on a small, WEIRD sample; the second is wider but vaguer. Amara judges the first stronger on balance, and says why. This is evaluation.

Both students understood the interpretation. Only Amara weighed its relative value against an alternative, with reasons.
generatedProse.summary: In psychology, evaluation means weighing the relative value of an interpretation against alternatives, with reasons drawn from the evidence, rather than judging it in isolation. You can now tell evaluation apart from analysis and choose an evaluative question to ask of a study. The next lesson completes the set: synthesis draws several evaluated sources together into an argument of your own.

check.body: In the worked example, what did Amara do that Tom did not?

items.text: She weighed the interpretation against a rival and judged which better fit the evidence, with reasons.
She separated the interpretation into its claim, evidence and reasoning.
She summarised the interpretation more accurately.
She quoted the original study more fully.

feedback.correct: That's right. Weighing the interpretation against a rival, with reasons, is evaluation.
feedback.incorrectNotFinal: Not quite. Tom already took the interpretation apart. Look for what Amara ADDED.
feedback.incorrectFinal: Amara evaluated: weighing the interpretation against an alternative and judging which better fit the evidence, with reasons. Both had already analysed it.
